title: Body, soul, mind
hook: the body senses, the soul desires, the mind rules (Meditations 3.16)

segments.voice: Yesterday: you won't read your notes. Your line was help yourself now. Which saved piece of advice did you finally use? Day five hundred forty-nine.

Picture a carriage. A driver up front, two horses pulling, the wooden body rattling along. Plato used a picture like that for the human being. Marcus Aurelius, closing his third book, offers a plainer one, with no horses at all. You are three things, he says: a body, a soul, and a mind. Each has its own job. And then he asks a hard question: which of those three jobs is actually yours alone? His answer is not the one most of us would guess. Today: body, soul, mind.
screen: `A CARRIAGE, A DRIVER, TWO HORSES.` → `MARCUS: THREE THINGS.` → `WHICH JOB IS YOURS ALONE?`

segments.voice: First, the three. Body, soul, mind, Marcus writes. To the body belong the senses. To the soul, which for him means the life force that wants and moves, belong the impulses. To the mind belong the principles. Second, the surprise. Then he checks each job against who else has it. Receiving impressions through the senses? Cattle do that. Being yanked around by desire? Wild animals do that, he says, and so did the cruelest tyrants of history, like Nero. Even using the mind to pursue what seems useful? People who betray their country and do anything behind closed doors do that too. None of the three, by itself, makes a good person. Third, what's left. So what belongs to the good person alone? Marcus answers: to welcome what happens and what's woven for them; to keep the spirit within untroubled and undisturbed by a crowd of impressions; to follow it quietly as a god; never to say anything false or do anything unjust. Fourth, a check-in, not a ranking. This isn't contempt for the body or for desire. The Stoics thought both were natural and needed. Marcus's point is about who drives. Senses report. Desires pull. Principles decide. When the order flips, and the pull decides, things go badly. That closes book three. It began with time running short, and it ends with the one thing worth spending that time on: a mind that keeps its own counsel, honestly, whatever comes.
screen: `SENSES, IMPULSES, PRINCIPLES.` · `CATTLE, BEASTS AND TRAITORS SHARE THEM.` · `WHAT'S LEFT: WELCOME, CALM, TRUTH.` · `WHO DRIVES?` · then, large: `THREE PARTS.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Check in with each of the three. Body first: what are your senses reporting? Warmth, an ache, the sound in the room. Just notice. Then the soul, the part that wants: what's pulling at you right now? Food, your phone, a worry, a person? Just notice. Then the mind: what principle would you choose to steer by for the next hour? Let it take the reins, gently. The bell holds the time.
Body, soul, mind. Marcus says the body senses, the soul desires, the mind holds principles, and the good person lets the mind steer. Today's word.
Your line: three parts. Three times today, check all three: what do I sense, what do I want, what will I choose? Day five hundred forty-nine.

howItsDone: Readers of Marcus Aurelius sometimes use Meditations 3.16 as a quick check-in: what the body senses, what the soul wants, and which principle the mind will steer by.

myth: Marcus says the body and desire are evil
the Stoics thought both natural; his point is about which part steers.
Marcus says even traitors use the mind to pursue what seems useful
so the mind's cleverness alone doesn't make a good person.
book three ends here, before the fire of book four.

fork.setup: you're tired, a craving is pulling hard, and your mind already knows what it wants to do. who gets the reins, in 3.16?
options: the impulse: it's strongest right now.
the mind, steering by a principle.
fork.reveal: Marcus: senses report, impulses pull, principles decide. the good person's part is letting the mind drive.

original.note: Greek: body, soul, mind, the three parts Marcus names in 3.16.

trapdoor: what you thought: the mind should control the body.
what it means: senses and desires belong even to animals and tyrants; what's yours alone is welcoming what comes and keeping truth and justice.
what a scholar hears: Marcus's soma, psyche, nous splits the soul into a life principle and a ruling mind, a later Stoic way of speaking.

notes: 3.16 paraphrased: body, soul, intelligence; to the body belong sensations, to the soul appetites (impulses), to the intelligence principles; receiving impressions belongs also to cattle; being pulled by desire to wild beasts, to effeminate men, to Phalaris and Nero; having the intelligence guide to what seems suitable to those who don't believe in gods, betray their country, and do their impure deeds behind closed doors; what is peculiar to the good man is to be pleased and content with what happens, not defile the divinity within, keep it tranquil, following it as a god, saying nothing contrary to truth, doing nothing contrary to justice. Confirm.
Plato's chariot image is a chariot with a charioteer and two winged horses (Phaedrus); the hook says 'carriage' loosely. Confirm acceptable.
3.16 as the last entry of book three: confirm against Long's numbering.
The trapdoor's claim about Marcus's tripartite soma/psyche/nous as a later Stoic usage: confirm wording.
